title: AQ Podcast | Colombia: An Early Test for the New Government
gist: Abelardo de la Espriella took office as Colombia's president on August 7, 2026 after a razor-thin election, then had his hardline, Milei-style agenda immediately upended when a 7.4-magnitude earthquake caused ~$10 billion in damage and forced him to declare a national emergency in his first week.

insights.claim: Abelardo de la Espriella was inaugurated as Colombia's president on August 7, 2026 after winning an extremely tight election, with over 26 million votes cast in the second round.
insights.speaker: Americas Quarterly
insights.so_what: A narrow-mandate presidency has limited political capital to force through a radical agenda, raising execution risk for investors watching Colombian policy direction.
insights.quote: Abelardo de la Espriella was inaugurated as Colombia’s new president after winning an incredibly tight election.

insights.claim: De la Espriella campaigned on a sharp break from outgoing president Gustavo Petro's four years in office, signaling a rightward, market-oriented policy pivot for Colombia.
insights.speaker: Americas Quarterly
insights.so_what: A Petro-to-de-la-Espriella swing reprices Colombian assets around deregulation and security, but only if the new government can actually govern.

insights.claim: A 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia three days after the August 2026 presidential inauguration, causing damages close to $10 billion and devastating hundreds of municipalities across 15 departments.
insights.speaker: Americas Quarterly
insights.so_what: A ~$10B disaster hitting in week one blows a hole in fiscal-consolidation plans and could force emergency spending that contradicts the promised austerity.
insights.quote: a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck the western part of the country, leaving damages close to $10 billion and devastating hundreds of municipalities across 15 departments

insights.claim: Instead of launching his promised reform program, de la Espriella's first major act as president was declaring a state of national emergency in response to the earthquake.
insights.speaker: Americas Quarterly
insights.so_what: An external shock forcing an emergency footing in week one delays the entire policy agenda and is the central variable for how much of the campaign platform survives.
insights.quote: Instead, his first major act was declaring a state of national emergency.

insights.claim: De la Espriella came to power promising Milei-style fiscal cuts and a hardline security plan for Colombia.
insights.speaker: Americas Quarterly
insights.so_what: Explicit modeling on Milei's shock-therapy playbook sets the template investors should benchmark Colombian fiscal execution against.

insights.claim: De la Espriella's agenda included restarting oil exploration in Colombia, reversing a signature policy stance of the Petro administration.
insights.speaker: Americas Quarterly
insights.so_what: Restarting oil exploration is a direct catalyst for Colombian energy and Ecopetrol-linked exposure if the new government follows through post-emergency.

insights.claim: De la Espriella promised to end Colombia's total peace process and launch joint military operations with the United States, marking a security and foreign-policy realignment toward Washington.
insights.speaker: Americas Quarterly
insights.so_what: Ending 'total peace' and partnering militarily with the US signals a harder security posture and closer US alignment, relevant to regional risk and counternarcotics flows.

insights.claim: Former Colombian finance minister and presidential candidate Mauricio Cárdenas, now Senior Scholar at Columbia University, is the analyst brought in to assess how much of de la Espriella's agenda on security, the economy and fiscal policy remains achievable.
insights.speaker: Americas Quarterly
insights.so_what: A former finance minister's read on post-earthquake fiscal room is the signal to track for whether Colombia's austerity plan is still viable.
